engine: redb 4.4.0 (pure Rust, single-file copy-on-write B-tree; no C toolchain; version pinned in Cargo.lock)
method: real embedded KV store: values are codec outputs stored under increasing u64 ids and decoded byte-exact on read; the shared trained dictionary is stored once under a metadata key and included in the footprint; footprint_bytes is measured after Database::compact() (steady state) and footprint_bytes_as_loaded is the copy-on-write size before compaction; write_amp = process wchar (write-syscall bytes) / logical bytes over the load; storage_bytes_per_get = process rchar delta per get; cold = first pass after reopen, warm = after a warm-up pass; cache_bytes is between the smallest and largest store so residency is a real effect

ledger_reference.name: ekbloom-m9-ledger (record-granular store, counting pread = central-ledger analogue)

verdict: Inside a real embedded KV engine (redb), on skewed 100-byte point gets: raw is fastest (130 ns warm p50) and smallest-unit; lz4-block stores 0.819x raw; zstd-dict stores 0.525x raw and its tail is 441 ns p99.9; EKBLOOM machine 9 stores 0.973x raw, decodes a get in 1072 ns warm p50 with a 2574 ns p99.9 tail and returns 592 B/get from storage (cold). Write amplification: raw 2.32x, lz4 1.63x, zstd-dict 0.95x, ekbloom-m9 1.94x. Range scan: raw 2430 MiB/s, lz4 1453, zstd-dict 595, ekbloom-m9 97. Verdict: machine 9 is a legitimate record-granular store (small footprint premium, decode-on-read) but it does NOT beat zstd-dict or LZ4 inside a real B-tree store on footprint, scan throughput, or write amplification; its only edge is the small, self-contained per-value tail, and even that depends on the engine's read path, not on the codec alone.
